title: Visual Arts
description: Ten texts about the visual arts: painting a fresco, restoring an old portrait, a photography review, a sculptor, printmaking, a street-art festival, how museums buy art, color theory, Degas and his dancers, and a town choosing a memorial.

lessons.title: How a Fresco Is Painted
lessons.summary: An explanation of how the old wall paintings in a small chapel were made on wet plaster, one day at a time.
lessons.text:
In a small stone chapel in the hills of central Italy, every wall is covered with paintings that are more than five hundred years old. Most of them tell stories from scripture, scene after scene, the way a book tells a story page by page. The largest scenes are in the sanctuary, the holiest part of the church. Around all of them runs a painted border of green vines, with small birds sitting among the vines.

These paintings are frescoes. The word comes from the Italian for "fresh," because a fresco is painted on fresh, wet plaster. The method explains a great deal about how the chapel looks.

The work began long before any color touched the wall. First, workers covered the stone with a rough layer of plaster. On it, the master painter drew his whole plan in red-brown paint. The chapel's architectural features, such as its windows, its doors and the curve of its ceiling, dictated where each scene could go. A window cannot be painted over, so the scenes had to be arranged around it. Even the narrow arch of the sanctuary dictated the shape of the pictures inside it.

Next, for each scene, the painter made a full-size drawing on heavy paper, called a cartoon. With a needle, an assistant poked small holes along every line of it, thousands of them.

Then speed began to matter. Every morning, a worker spread a thin layer of fresh plaster over only the part of the wall that could be finished that day. The assistant held the cartoon against the wet surface and lightly tapped a small bag of black dust over the holes he had poked. When the paper was removed, rows of tiny black dots remained. The painter mixed his colors with nothing but water and brushed them lightly onto the wet plaster. As it dried, the colors became part of the wall itself. Thereafter, they could not be changed or washed away. If the painter made a serious mistake, the only cure was to cut out the plaster and paint that section again the next day.

Look closely today and you can still see the edges of these daily patches. One scene on the left wall needed twelve of them. It shows a knight on a white horse, his lance raised, riding to rescue a young girl whom robbers have kidnapped. The story comes not from scripture but from a local legend. The painter gave the kidnapped girl a calm face and painted the long lance as one straight line across three daily patches.

Questions:
Why is this kind of painting called a fresco?
It is called a fresco because the word comes from the Italian for "fresh," and the painting is done on fresh, wet plaster.
What dictated where each scene could go?
The architectural features of the chapel, such as its windows, its doors and its ceiling, dictated where each scene could go.
Why did the assistant poke holes in the cartoon?
He poked holes so that black dust could pass through them and leave the lines of the drawing on the wall.
What happened to the colors after the plaster dried?
The colors became part of the wall, and thereafter they could not be changed or washed away.
What does the scene on the left wall show?
It shows a knight with a lance riding to rescue a girl whom robbers have kidnapped.

lessons.title: The Restorer and the Lace Collar
lessons.summary: A restorer spends months cleaning an old Dutch portrait, slowly and carefully, until the white lace appears again.
lessons.text:
When the portrait arrived at Clara Weiss's studio, the woman in it seemed to be wearing a brown collar. The painting was Dutch, from around 1650, and it showed a serious young woman in a black dress. Clara suspected that the collar was not brown at all. In the Netherlands at that time, wealthy women wore wide collars of white lace, and painters were proud of how well they could paint lace.

The brown color came from the varnish, a clear protective layer that painters brush over a finished picture. Over the centuries, many old varnishes slowly decay. As they decay, they turn yellow and then brown, and everything beneath them looks darker and dirtier than it really is. Clara's job was to remove this old layer without harming a single line of the original paint.

Before she touched the surface, she made a thorough study of the painting. She inspected it under strong light, under a magnifying glass and under special lamps that reveal old repairs. This thorough examination showed her two areas, near the hands, where a later restorer had added new paint. Using a tiny sample from the edge, a scientist helped her verify what the old varnish was made of. Only after she could verify this did she choose her cleaning liquids.

Many of these liquids are harmful in two ways. Some are harmful to old paint if they are too strong, and some are harmful to people who breathe them, so Clara worked under a fan that continuously pulled the air away from her face. She tested each liquid on a tiny corner first. Then she began to clean with small rolls of cotton on wooden sticks, inspecting each roll to see whether any color had come off.

Some of her most useful tools were bought from a company that supplies dentists. A dentist's mirror let her look at the painting from an angle, and a dentist's thin steel pick removed bits of old dirt from the deep lines of the paint. "They are made for careful work in small spaces," she explained.

The cleaning took almost four months. Work of this kind always seems to consume more time than anyone expects, and a single difficult corner can consume a whole week, so Clara did not hurry. Day by day, the collar changed from brown to cream and finally to white. Every thread of the lace appeared again.

One rule guided her continuously: a restorer must never erase the history of a painting. She did not erase the small cracks of age, and every new touch of paint she added could be removed by a future restorer. Her aim was not to make the portrait look new, but to let it look like itself again.

Questions:
Why did the collar look brown?
It looked brown because the old varnish had decayed and turned yellow and then brown.
How did Clara study the painting before cleaning it?
She made a thorough study and inspected it under strong light, a magnifying glass and special lamps.
Why did she work under a fan?
Some cleaning liquids are harmful to breathe, so the fan continuously pulled the air away from her face.
What tools did she buy from a company that supplies dentists?
She bought a dentist's mirror and a dentist's thin steel pick.
What rule guided Clara's work?
She believed that a restorer must never erase the history of a painting.

lessons.title: Review: Life at the Edges
lessons.summary: A review of a photography exhibition about animals in the far north, from swans and geese to a diving falcon.
lessons.text:
Rarely does a photography exhibition make visitors stand so still. "Life at the Edges," now showing at the Harbor Gallery, brings together sixty photographs by Mara Lind, who has spent the last twelve years working in the polar regions. It is a quiet, serious show, and it is worth the trip.

The exhibition is arranged by geographic region, moving from the warmer edge of the north toward the ice itself. This geographic order works well. As you walk through the rooms, the colors slowly disappear, until the final room is almost entirely white, gray and blue. You feel that you are traveling north with the photographer.

The first room is about birds. Lind photographs swans on the lakes of the summer tundra, where they come to nest. In one large print, a pair of white swans stands beside a nest in the soft evening light, and the swans' reflection in the water is so clear that the picture seems to have two skies. Nearby is a picture of migration: countless snow geese rising from a field at once. The geese fill the frame from edge to edge, and only after a minute do you notice a single goose flying in the opposite direction.

The most striking image, however, is of a falcon. The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth; in a dive, it can reach more than 200 miles per hour. To capture that velocity, Lind waited for days on a cliff and used an extremely fast shutter. The result shows the falcon with its wings folded, sharp in every feather, while the rocks behind it are only a soft blur. It is a picture about velocity itself.

The second half of the show turns to the sea. Lind joined a team of scientists who used a small research submarine to explore the water under the ice. The submarine photographs, lit only by its lamps, show strange pale creatures and a world that very few people have seen. These are not dramatic pictures, but they are some of the most beautiful in the show.

The last room is the hardest. Here we see the polar ecosystem under pressure: thin ice, a hungry polar bear walking along an empty shore, and a fierce storm hiding the horizon. Lind does not lecture. The wall texts explain, simply and clearly, how each animal depends on the others, and how a change in the ice affects the whole ecosystem.

My one complaint is that the lighting in the second room is too dark to see the smaller prints well. Otherwise, this is a fierce and honest exhibition, made with great patience. Go early, and give it time.

Questions:
How is the exhibition arranged?
It is arranged by geographic region, moving from the warmer edge of the north toward the ice.
What does the photograph of migration show?
It shows countless snow geese rising from a field, and one goose flying in the opposite direction.
How did Lind capture the velocity of the falcon?
She waited for days on a cliff and used an extremely fast shutter.
Where were the photographs of the sea taken?
They were taken under the ice from a small research submarine.
What is the reviewer's one complaint?
The lighting in the second room is too dark to see the smaller prints well.

lessons.title: Profile: The Artist of Spirals
lessons.summary: A profile of a sculptor who spent two years and ten models on one large steel spiral.
lessons.text:
Ines Varga is renowned for one shape. For thirty years, she has made spirals: small spirals of copper wire, tall spirals of wood and, more recently, enormous spirals of steel that rise above city squares. Today she is one of the most renowned artists in her country, but she still works in the same old workshop at the edge of town, with two assistants and a gray cat.

I visited her there on a cold morning in the spring. The workshop, which was built long ago to store grain, is a large circular room, and its circular walls are covered with drawings. "A spiral is a circle that refuses to close," she told me. "It keeps moving. That is why I never get bored with it."

Varga is a believer in slow work. Every large sculpture begins as a prototype, a small model that lets her test the idea before she spends money on steel. The first prototype is usually made of paper. The next ones are made of wood or thin metal. Each prototype teaches her something about balance, weight and light.

Her latest work, a spiral forty feet high for a new hospital garden, needed more prototypes than any sculpture before it. The problem was the wind. A tall spiral catches the wind like a sail, and the engineers were worried that it might bend. The first nine prototypes all failed in some way. One was too heavy at the top, and another looked beautiful but would not stand safely.

"It was frustrating," Varga admitted. "The most frustrating thing was that I knew exactly what I wanted to see, and I could not make it stand up." Some friends told her that two years on a single shape was madness. She laughed when I repeated the word. "Perhaps it is a kind of madness," she said, "but it is a very patient madness."

The tenth prototype finally worked. In the tenth model, the spiral grows thinner as it rises, and a circular steel base, hidden under the ground, holds it steady. The engineers tested it, and they were satisfied.

Her assistants speak about her dedication with real admiration. During the final month, Varga caught the flu, but she still came to the workshop every day, wrapped in a heavy coat, to watch the welding. "We sent her home twice," one assistant said, smiling. "The flu did not stop her, and neither did we."

Varga does not like to talk about dedication. "I am simply a believer in patience," she said. "And I am curious. I want to know what the next spiral will look like." The hospital spiral was put up in the autumn, and patients can see it from their windows, changing slowly from gold to gray during the day.

Questions:
What shape is Ines Varga renowned for?
She is renowned for spirals.
What is a prototype, and why does Varga make one?
A prototype is a small model, and she makes one to test her idea before she spends money on steel.
Why did the hospital spiral need so many prototypes?
It needed many prototypes because a tall spiral catches the wind, and the engineers were worried it might bend.
Which prototype finally worked?
The tenth prototype finally worked.
How did Varga show her dedication when she caught the flu?
She still came to the workshop every day to watch the welding.

lessons.title: Printmaking Explained
lessons.summary: An explanation of how prints are made, why each one counts as an original, and how editions are kept honest.
lessons.text:
Many visitors to a gallery presume that a print is simply a copy, like a poster of a famous painting. They presume this because prints often come in many nearly identical sheets. In fact, a print made by an artist is an original work of art. The difference lies in how it is made.

In printmaking, the artist does not paint directly on the paper. Instead, the artist prepares a surface, such as a block of wood or a sheet of metal, puts ink on it and presses paper against it. In a woodcut, the artist cuts away the parts of the block that should stay white, and the raised parts carry the ink. In an etching, the artist draws lines through a thin protective layer on a metal plate, and acid bites those lines into the metal. The ink is pushed into the lines, the surface is wiped clean, and a heavy press forces the paper against the plate.

In a screen print, the artist pushes ink through a fine screen, one color at a time. A print of bright red and blue stripes needs at least two screens: one for the red stripes and one for the blue. Screen printing can produce colors so bright and clean that they shine like jewels. One printmaker calls her favorite inks "my jewel box."

Because the block or plate can print many sheets, artists usually decide in advance how many they will make. This group of prints is called an edition. The artist must specify its size, and the number is written in pencil at the bottom of each sheet: "12/50" means the twelfth print of an edition of fifty. Many galleries ask artists to specify, explicitly and in writing, that no more prints will be made. Some artists then cut a line across the plate, to uphold that promise. Collectors depend on these rules, and the whole market works only if artists and galleries uphold them.

An artist may also modify the plate between printings, adding a line here or removing a shadow there. Modifying a plate substantially creates a new "state" of the work, and prints made before and after the change are counted separately.

Printmaking has a long history of wide circulation. In nineteenth-century Japan, woodblock prints were sold cheaply, and some were printed in thousands of copies. Their circulation was so wide that ordinary people could buy them as easily as a packet of tea. Later, when these prints reached Europe, they substantially changed how many painters thought about color and design.

Today, a print often arrives at its buyer in a flat packet with a short note explaining the edition. That note states explicitly how many prints exist, and that number is part of what makes each one valuable.

Questions:
What do many visitors presume about prints?
They presume that a print is simply a copy, like a poster.
How is a print of red and blue stripes made?
It needs at least two screens, one for the red stripes and one for the blue.
What does "12/50" mean on a print?
It means the twelfth print of an edition of fifty.
Why do some artists cut a line across the plate?
They do it to uphold the promise that no more prints will be made.
How wide was the circulation of woodblock prints in nineteenth-century Japan?
Some were printed in thousands of copies, and ordinary people could buy them as easily as a packet of tea.

lessons.title: A Weekend of Street Art
lessons.summary: The organizer of a street-art festival explains how her team turned an old boulevard into an open-air gallery for everyone.
lessons.text:
Every September, for one weekend, North Boulevard turns into the largest gallery in the city. The street-art festival began six years ago with four artists and a few cans of paint. This year, it brought together forty artists and more than twenty thousand visitors. Its main organizer, Rosa Delgado, a former art teacher, explained how the festival works.

The boulevard was a natural choice. It is wide and long, and along its sides stand rows of plain brick walls and several empty billboards. "For years, those billboards were just faded advertisements," Delgado said. "We asked the owners if artists could paint them, and most of them agreed." Now each billboard carries a new painting every year, and people drive down the boulevard just to see them.

The organizers work hard to make the festival inclusive. Entry is free, every artwork can be seen from the street, and there are guides who describe the paintings for visitors who cannot see well. One corner is set aside for children. There, toddlers can draw on the ground with large pieces of colored chalk while their parents watch. "A toddler with a piece of chalk is an artist too," Delgado said. "An inclusive festival should start with the youngest people."

Not all the art is painted. A group of retired women from the neighborhood spends the whole year knitting. They knit long, colorful covers for the trees and the street lamps, and on the first morning of the festival, the boulevard is suddenly full of knitted stripes and flowers. Visitors take more photographs of the trees than of anything else.

Some of the most serious work is made by teenagers. This year, students from a local high school painted a long wall beside the recreational center, where many young people play basketball after school. The center offers recreational programs for teenagers, and its director invited the students to use the wall. Their painting is about bullying. It shows a line of students, and one of them is standing alone; along the wall, step by step, the others turn toward the lonely student and offer a hand. The students wanted every victim of bullying to see that someone is on their side.

Because parking is limited, the organizers run a free shuttle from the train station every fifteen minutes. The shuttle buses are themselves painted by artists, so the trip becomes part of the show.

What makes the festival memorable, Delgado believes, is that people meet the artists face to face. Visitors can watch a painting grow over two days, ask questions and come back to see the result. "That is the most memorable part for most people," she said. "They see that art is work, done by ordinary people with real skill."

Questions:
Why was North Boulevard a natural choice for the festival?
It is wide and long, and it has plain brick walls and several empty billboards.
How do the organizers make the festival inclusive?
Entry is free, the art can be seen from the street, guides describe paintings, and there is a corner for children.
What do the retired women knit?
They knit long, colorful covers for the trees and the street lamps.
What is the students' painting about?
It is about bullying, and it shows students offering a hand to a lonely student.
How can visitors get to the festival without a car?
They can take a free shuttle from the train station every fifteen minutes.

lessons.title: How a Museum Decides What to Buy
lessons.summary: A look at how a small maritime museum chooses, checks and pays for a new painting for its collection.
lessons.text:
Visitors often presume that museums buy whatever they like. In reality, buying a work of art is a slow process with many rules, especially for a small museum. The Bayport Maritime Museum, which tells the history of ships, sailors and the sea, offers a good example.

The museum's money for new works is limited. Each year, the city gives it a subsidy for its daily costs, such as heating, guards and cleaning. That subsidy may not be used for buying art. For new works, the museum has a separate yearly allowance from a private fund, and this allowance is small: about the price of a used car. Every purchase must therefore be chosen with great care.

The process starts with a proposal. A member of staff suggests a work and explains why it belongs in the collection. A good proposal answers three questions. Does the work tell part of the museum's maritime story? Is it in good condition? And do we know where it has been since it was made? The last question is essential. Museums are forbidden by law from buying stolen works, and under international agreements it is also forbidden to buy objects that were taken illegally out of their home countries. Before any purchase, researchers trace the work's history, owner by owner.

Next, a committee compares all the proposals for the year. Often this is a process of elimination. A painting may be beautiful but in poor condition; a model ship may be interesting but too similar to one the museum already owns. Step by step, through careful elimination, the list grows shorter until only one or two works remain.

Famous names tempt every museum. "It is easy to be tempted by a big name," said the director, Paul Brennan, who is near the end of a twelve-year tenure. "But a famous painting that has nothing to do with our story would be a poor use of public trust." During his tenure, the museum has bought only fourteen works.

Some critics argue that capitalism has turned art into an investment, and that prices now say more about wealth than about quality. Brennan sees both sides. "Capitalism created the market that lets us buy art at all," he said, "but it also means we cannot compete with the richest collectors. So we look where they do not look."

Sometimes the museum is simply fortunate. Last year, the family of a deceased sea captain offered his collection of drawings of the harbor. The deceased captain had made them himself over forty years. The museum was fortunate twice: the family asked a fair price, and the drawings filled a real gap in the collection.

Questions:
What may the city's subsidy not be used for?
It may not be used for buying art.
What three questions does a good proposal answer?
It explains whether the work tells part of the maritime story, whether it is in good condition, and where it has been since it was made.
Why does the committee's work often become a process of elimination?
Some works are in poor condition or too similar to works the museum owns, so the list grows shorter step by step.
How many works has the museum bought during Brennan's tenure?
It has bought only fourteen works.
Why was the museum fortunate last year?
The family of a deceased sea captain offered his drawings at a fair price, and they filled a gap in the collection.

lessons.title: Color Theory for Beginners
lessons.summary: A beginner learns from an online tutorial why colors on a screen and colors in paint mix in opposite ways.
lessons.text:
When Sam decided to learn to paint, his first problem was color. He mixed his paints randomly, hoping for a good result, and he usually ended up with a muddy brown. So one evening he opened his browser and searched for a beginner's tutorial on color theory. He found a clear one, made by a painting teacher, and watched it on his desktop computer. These are the main ideas he learned.

Color begins in the eye. At the back of the human eye are millions of cells called cones, which react to light. Most people have three types of cones, sensitive to long, medium and short waves of light, which we see roughly as red, green and blue. Every color we see is the brain's reading of how strongly each type of cone reacts.

Screens use this fact. A phone, a desktop monitor or an old plasma television makes every color from tiny points of red, green and blue light. The tutorial suggested an experiment: open a white page in your browser, take a screenshot, and enlarge the screenshot many times. On some screens, including older plasma screens, you can see the tiny points of color. Where all three shine at full strength, we see white. Light, in other words, adds up: the more colors you mix, the brighter the result.

Paint obeys the opposite rule. Paint does not give off light; it absorbs part of the light that falls on it and reflects the rest. When you mix two paints, each one absorbs more of the light, so the mixture becomes darker. This is why Sam's random mixtures turned brown. All colors obey these rules, and a painter who understands them can predict the result instead of guessing.

The tutorial then explained the color wheel. Red, yellow and blue sit at three points of the circle. Between them are orange, green and violet, and each of these has two constituent colors: orange, for example, is made of red and yellow. Knowing the constituent colors of a mixture helps you make it again. Colors that sit across from each other on the wheel, such as blue and orange, make each other look stronger when they are placed side by side.

Sam watched the most difficult part of the tutorial three times. Each time, he stopped the video, tried the mixture himself and then pressed replay. The replay button, he decided, was the best teacher of all.

The next weekend, he painted a small picture of an orange boat on a blue lake. He chose his colors on purpose, not randomly, and he mixed each one from no more than two constituent paints. For the first time, the colors were clean.

Questions:
Why did Sam's paintings turn muddy brown at first?
He mixed his paints randomly, and mixing many paints makes the result darker.
What are cones?
Cones are cells at the back of the eye that react to light.
What experiment did the tutorial suggest?
It suggested opening a white page in a browser, taking a screenshot and enlarging it to see the tiny points of color.
What are the constituent colors of orange?
The constituent colors of orange are red and yellow.
Why did Sam press replay?
He pressed replay to watch the most difficult part of the tutorial again after trying each mixture.

lessons.title: Degas and the Dancers
lessons.summary: An account of why Edgar Degas drew dancers and racehorses, and how critics first received his famous wax dancer.
lessons.text:
Few artists are connected with a single subject as closely as Edgar Degas is connected with ballet. The French artist, who lived from 1834 to 1917, made hundreds of paintings, drawings and pastels of dancers. Yet it is worth asking what exactly interested him, because the answer is not as simple as a love of pretty costumes.

What fascinated Degas was the body at work. He rarely painted a ballet at its most glamorous moment. Instead, he went to rehearsals and classes at the Paris Opera, and he drew dancers stretching, waiting, tying their shoes or resting with tired faces. On stage, the dancers looked light and effortless under the blaze of the lights. Behind the stage, Degas saw the long hours of practice that made that effortless look possible. His pictures often show both worlds: the blaze of color on the stage and the plain, shadowy rooms where the work was done.

The same interest led him to the racetrack. Degas also painted horse races, and his pictures show jockeys, nervous horses and the grooms who cared for them. A groom leading a horse before a race and a young dancer warming up before a class were, for Degas, two versions of one subject: a trained body preparing to perform.

He was also aware of the social world of the ballet. Many of the young dancers came from poor families, and dancing was a way to earn money. Socially, they stood far below the wealthy men in evening suits who often appear at the edges of his pictures, men who were socially powerful and free to walk behind the stage. Degas did not make speeches about this, but he painted it honestly, and the contrast is easy to see.

His most famous dancer is a sculpture. In 1881, he showed a wax figure of a young ballet student, about two-thirds of life size. It was dressed in a real cloth skirt and a real silk ribbon, and it had real hair. Many critics were shocked. Some condemned the figure as ugly, and others condemned the realism of the real clothes. Degas never exhibited the sculpture again.

Fortunately, the wax figure survived in his studio. After his death, bronze copies were made, and today they stand in museums around the world. Visitors now see what the critics who condemned it could not: a tired, proud girl standing very straight, as she had been taught.

Fortunately, too, Degas kept working even when his eyesight grew weak in later life. He turned more to pastels and to sculpture, which he could shape with his hands. Until the end, his subject remained the same: bodies shaped by training and by work.

Questions:
What interested Degas about ballet?
He was interested in the body at work, including the long hours of practice behind the stage.
Why did Degas also paint horse races?
He saw jockeys, horses and grooms as another version of a trained body preparing to perform.
How were the young dancers different socially from the wealthy men in his pictures?
Many dancers came from poor families, so socially they stood far below the wealthy men.
How did critics react to the wax dancer in 1881?
Many were shocked, and some condemned the figure as ugly.
What happened to the wax figure after Degas died?
Bronze copies were made, and today they stand in museums around the world.

lessons.title: Two Designs for One Memorial
lessons.summary: A town compares two designs for a new memorial, one realistic and one simple, and weighs what each can say.
lessons.text:
In the center of the town of Millbrook stands an old stone soldier. He was put up more than a hundred years ago to remember the members of the local militia who died in an early war, and the words cut into the base read "Faithful unto death." Now the town wants a second memorial, for the men and women from Millbrook who served in the wars of the last century. Two designs have reached the final round, and the town council has invited citizens to compare them.

The first design is realistic. It is a group of bronze figures, life size: an infantry soldier carrying a wounded friend, a nurse, and an artillery crew loading a heavy gun. The details are explicit. You can see the weight of the infantry soldier's pack, the mud on his boots and the effort in the faces of the artillery crew. Its supporters say that this explicit realism is its strength. "People should see what war cost," one older resident wrote. "A memorial ought to show it plainly."

Realistic memorials have a long history. Nearly two thousand years ago, the Romans built a tall column in their capital, with a carved band that winds around it like a spiral. The carvings show Roman legions crossing rivers, building camps and fighting. Even today, you can follow the legions from the bottom of the column to the top, scene by scene.

The second design is simple: a low wall of dark stone, curving gently across the lawn, with the names of the dead cut into it. There are no figures at all. Its supporters point to a famous example, the national memorial for the Vietnam War in Washington, which also uses a dark wall of names. When that design was chosen in 1981, some critics were quick to condemn it as cold and empty. Today it is one of the most visited memorials in the country, and many visitors touch the names.

Each side has its worries, although nobody in Millbrook wants to condemn the other side's choice. Critics of the bronze group respect its honesty, but they believe it is too explicit for small children, who play in the square every day. Critics of the wall fear that it will disrupt the open lawn, where the market is held on weekends, and some feel that a list of names, without any image, says too little. The supporters of the wall reply that it would disrupt very little, since people could still walk around it.

The council will decide next spring. Whatever it chooses, the new memorial will stand near the old stone soldier, and both will carry the same idea, even if they express it differently. One old resident suggested that the new memorial should repeat the same three words: "Faithful unto death."

Questions:
Who does the old stone soldier remember?
He remembers the members of the local militia who died in an early war.
What does the first design show?
It shows an infantry soldier carrying a wounded friend, a nurse and an artillery crew loading a gun.
What do the carvings on the Roman column show?
They show Roman legions crossing rivers, building camps and fighting.
What worries critics of the bronze group?
They believe it is too explicit for small children who play in the square.
Why do some people think the wall would disrupt the square?
They fear it would disrupt the open lawn where the market is held on weekends.
